needs: not expressible: duty status as an operand (rl2:obligationStateOperand with rl2:targetNorm); written as a precondition instead
notes: RL2 gates ex:executeOrderPrivilege with a condition reading the derived status of ex:recordOrderDuty. due2 has no duty-status operand; the closest encoding, used here, is odrl:duty on the permission (the precondition reading). That is the encoding RL2 itself calls canonical for this pattern (check-signing-sod), and it gives the same decisions apart from the standing Pending/NotApplicable divergence (README). The duty is also an independent rl2:clause, so it is also an odrl:obligation of the policy; both roles share one instance (member scope, the default; same binding, since the duty declares its own assignee and inherits nothing). It is in force whenever the permission matches the request, and its status corresponds to RL2's duty status: fulfilled ↔ Fulfilled, outstanding ↔ Active (no window, so never Violated). RL2's 'audit record for that order' is not modelled in RL2 either (the duty's object is the fixed ex:AuditRecord), so one record serves every execution; grant scope would bind it per request, but then scenario 1 would be Pending because ex:ev1 carries no discharges. Scenarios 3 and 4 are added.

expected.why: ex:executeOrderPrivilege applies. ex:ev1 is a witness for ex:recordOrderDuty: actor is its assignee ex:Trader, action and object match, and it occurred before effective_at. The duty has no constraints, so it is T and the candidate is ready. The same duty as an obligation is in force (the permission matches) and fulfilled by the same witness.

The permission applies; ex:recordOrderDuty has no witness, so it is F (outstanding). The only alternative is pending; no deadline, so it is never violated. The obligation is in force and outstanding (RL2: Active).
ex:ev2's actor is not the duty's assignee ex:Trader, so it is not a witness. With no witness the duty is F and the candidate pending; the obligation is in force and outstanding.
